title: Why Economists Hate Trump's Tariff Plan | WSJ
summary: WSJ explainer (2024) on why economists dislike tariffs, using the chicken war and the 2018 washing machine and steel tariffs.

assertions.quote: They've gotta pass that price on to consumers who ultimately pay it.
not only did the price of imported washing machines go up, so did the ones made in the US
This is a very expensive job creation program.

verdicts.note: Studies of the washing machine and steel tariffs put the consumer cost per job created in the hundreds of thousands of dollars a year.

assertions.quote: you lose jobs as many if not more jobs in those downstream industries as you gain in the upstream industries
All the industries that use steel have to pay the higher price that squeezes their profit margins.
Tariffs are really hard to remove.

verdicts.note: The 1964 truck tariff still stands and the 2018 tariffs were kept by the next administration; concentrated beneficiaries defend them.

assertions.quote: So not only will US import shrink, but US exports will shrink as well.
about 5% of what the federal government currently brings in with taxes
it did motivate US companies to move out of China and made supply chains more resilient

verdicts.note: China's share of US imports fell sharply after 2018 as sourcing shifted to Vietnam, Mexico and elsewhere, though often via Chinese-owned plants.

After the 2018-2019 tariffs China's share of U.S. imports fell from nearly 25 percent to about 15 percent by 2024, and in 2025 it fell a further 5 points to below 10 percent, with Mexico and Vietnam gaining; the authors attribute the supply chain reorganisation to the higher tariff-inclusive import prices.

assertions.quote: But it didn't change much of China's behavior and in many ways they became more aggressive.

verdicts.note: China did not meet its Phase One purchase commitments and expanded industrial subsidies and export volumes after 2018.
